00Orientation

How this book works

Six parts, from "what is the JVM?" to "why is my server out of memory?" Read in order the first time; jump around when revising.

In Ramu's kitchen

Before Ramu's chai stall became a chain (that's the System Design book), it was one busy kitchen. The kitchen is our running picture for Java. The restaurant building is a process. The chefs are threads. The recipe cards are classes; the dishes made from them are objects. The storeroom shelves are the heap, each chef's personal notepad is their stack, and the cleaner who clears plates nobody uses is the garbage collector.

01Platform

How Java runs: JDK, JRE and the JVM

javac turns your code into bytecode; the JVM loads that bytecode and runs it, first by interpreting it, then by compiling the hot parts to native machine code.

In Ramu's kitchen

Ramu writes his recipes in Bengali. His new branches are in Chennai, Pune and Delhi, where cooks speak different languages. Instead of writing the recipe four times, he translates it once into a universal kitchen picture-language that every head cook in every city has been trained to read. Each head cook then reads the pictures and tells their own team what to do. Recipes the cook makes 500 times a day, he memorises completely so he no longer needs to look at the card.

Bengali recipe = .java source. Picture-language = bytecode. The trained head cook in each city = the JVM for each operating system. Memorising the popular recipes = the JIT compiler.

JDK, JRE, JVM: three boxes, one inside the other

From source to running program

  1. Compilejavac Order.java checks types and produces Order.class, containing platform-independent bytecode.
  2. LoadWhen the class is first needed, a class loader finds the .class file (bootstrap → platform → application loaders, parent first) and loads it into memory.
  3. LinkThe verifier checks the bytecode is safe; static fields get default values; symbolic references are resolved.
  4. InitialiseStatic initialisers run, once per class.
  5. ExecuteThe interpreter runs bytecode immediately. Methods called often become "hot" and the JIT (C1, then C2) compiles them to optimised native code.
  6. ManageWhile running, the garbage collector reclaims objects no one references.

Why the JIT matters

Interpreter

Starts instantly, runs every bytecode one by one. Slow for loops that run millions of times.

JIT (C1 → C2)

Profiles the running code and compiles hot methods to native code with optimisations: inlining, loop unrolling, escape analysis, removing unused locks.

Warm-up

A Java service is slower for its first seconds; that's why load tests "warm up" first. Java 25 adds ahead-of-time profiling to shorten this.

GraalVM native image

Compiles the whole app ahead of time into a native binary: very fast startup, lower memory, no JIT. Popular for serverless.

Common trap

"Java is interpreted, so it's slow." Modern JVMs compile hot code to native machine code, often as fast as C++ for long-running servers. What Java pays is startup time and memory, not steady-state speed.

Lock it in

Write, Compile, Load, Link, Init, Run, JIT.

JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM. Bytecode is the portable middle layer; the JVM per OS is what makes "write once, run anywhere" true. Hot code gets JIT-compiled to native.

Interview questions

Is Java compiled or interpreted?

Both. javac compiles source to bytecode ahead of time. At runtime the JVM interprets bytecode, and the JIT compiles frequently executed methods to native code. So it's a hybrid.

What is a class loader and what is parent delegation?

A class loader finds and loads .class files. Java has bootstrap (core classes), platform, and application (your classpath) loaders. Before loading a class, a loader first asks its parent; only if the parent can't find it does it load it itself. This stops your code from replacing core classes like java.lang.String.

Why is the main method public static void main(String[] args)?

public so the JVM can call it from outside the class, static so it can be called without creating an object, void because the exit code is returned via System.exit, and String[] for command-line arguments. (Java 25 also allows simpler instance main() methods in compact source files, mainly for learning and scripts.)

Next: Memory: stack, heap and references →
02Platform

Memory: stack, heap and references

Each thread has its own stack for method calls and local variables; all objects live on one shared heap. Variables hold references (addresses), not objects.

In Ramu's kitchen

Every chef carries a small notepad: what they're doing right now, quick numbers, and "the big pot is on shelf 7". When a chef finishes a task, they tear off that page. The actual pots and ingredients sit on the shared storeroom shelves, which every chef can reach. Two chefs can have "shelf 7" written on their notepads: both are pointing at the same pot.

Notepad = stack (one per thread, a page per method call). Storeroom = heap (shared). "Shelf 7" = a reference.

StackHeap
HoldsMethod frames: local primitives and referencesAll objects and arrays (and their fields)
Shared?No, one per threadYes, all threads
LifetimeFrame removed when the method returnsUntil no references remain, then GC
Error when fullStackOverflowError (deep recursion)OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Size flag-Xss-Xms (start) / -Xmx (max)

Java is always pass-by-value

The value passed for an object is the reference (a copy of the address). You can change the object it points to, but you can't make the caller's variable point somewhere else.

Common trap

"Objects are passed by reference in Java." No: references are passed by value. The swap function swap(a, b) on two objects can never swap the caller's variables in Java.

Lock it in

Notepad per chef, shelves for everyone.

Stack: per thread, frames, locals, fast, auto-cleaned. Heap: shared objects, GC-managed. Metaspace: class metadata. Java is always pass-by-value; for objects the value is a reference.

Interview questions

Where are static variables stored?

Static fields belong to the class. Since Java 8 they're stored with the class's Class object on the heap, while the class metadata itself lives in Metaspace (which replaced PermGen and uses native memory).

What causes StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError?

StackOverflowError: a thread's stack ran out of frames, usually unbounded recursion. OutOfMemoryError: the heap (or metaspace, or native memory for threads) couldn't satisfy an allocation even after GC, often from a memory leak or undersized -Xmx.

What is escape analysis?

A JIT optimisation: if an object never escapes a method (no reference leaves it), the JVM can avoid allocating it on the heap (scalar replacement) and remove locks on it. Small, short-lived objects can become almost free.

Next: Types, wrappers and casting →
03Platform

Types, wrappers and casting

Java has 8 primitive types that hold values directly, and objects that are reached by reference. Wrappers like Integer bridge the two, with a few famous traps.

In Ramu's kitchen

Small things like a pinch of salt go straight into the pot (a primitive: the value itself). Bigger things come in a labelled jar on a shelf, and the recipe just says which jar (an object reference). Sometimes a machine only accepts jars, so Ramu puts his pinch of salt into a tiny jar first. That's boxing.

PrimitiveSizeRange / noteWrapperDefault (field)
byte8 bit-128 to 127Byte0
short16 bit-32,768 to 32,767Short0
int32 bitabout ±2.1 billionInteger0
long64 bitabout ±9.2 × 1018Long0L
float32 bit~7 decimal digitsFloat0.0f
double64 bit~15 decimal digitsDouble0.0
char16 bita UTF-16 code unitCharacter'\u0000'
booleanJVM-dependenttrue / falseBooleanfalse

Local variables have no default: the compiler forces you to assign before use. Fields get the defaults above; object fields default to null.

Autoboxing and its traps

Casting, overflow and money

Widening is automatic

int → long → float → double needs no cast and never loses magnitude.

Narrowing needs a cast

(int) 3.99 is 3 (truncates). (byte) 200 is -56 (wraps around).

Silent overflow

Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 becomes negative. Use Math.addExact to throw instead, or long.

Floating point and money

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.30000000000000004. Use BigDecimal (from a String) for money.

Lock it in

"Be Smart In Life, For Decent Coffee Brews": byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean.

Compare wrappers with equals, never ==. Never unbox something that can be null. BigDecimal for money, long for big counts.

Interview questions

Why does Integer a = 100, b = 100; a == b print true but 1000 prints false?

Integer.valueOf (used by autoboxing) caches values from -128 to 127, so both variables reference the same cached object. Outside that range new objects are created, and == compares references, not values.

Why can't you use primitives in generics like List<int>?

Generics work with object references (type erasure turns T into Object). Primitives aren't objects, so you use wrappers (List<Integer>) or primitive-specialised types like IntStream to avoid boxing.

Next: Strings and the string pool →
04Platform

Strings and the string pool

A String can never change after it's created. That immutability makes strings safe to share, cache and use as map keys, and it's why you build long text with StringBuilder.

In Ramu's kitchen

The menu card on the wall is laminated. Nobody can scribble on it, so every waiter can point customers to the same card safely. If Ramu wants "Masala Chai" to read "Masala Chai (Large)", he prints a new card. Popular cards are kept in one card box (the string pool) so the kitchen never prints a duplicate of "Masala Chai".

Why immutable?

Safe sharing

The pool can hand the same object to everyone because nobody can change it.

Thread-safe for free

No locks needed to read a string from many threads.

Reliable map keys

The hash code is computed once and cached; a key can't change after you put it in a HashMap.

Security

A file path or DB URL you validated can't be swapped underneath you.

StringStringBuilderStringBuffer
Mutable?NoYesYes
Thread-safe?Yes (immutable)NoYes (synchronized)
Use forMost textBuilding text in one thread (almost always)Legacy code; rarely needed
Lock it in

Laminated card, one card box, a notebook for drafts.

String is immutable and pooled for literals. Compare with equals. Build text with StringBuilder, not += in loops.

Interview questions

How many objects does new String("chai") create?

Up to two: the literal "chai" in the string pool (if it isn't already there, created when the class is loaded) and one new String object on the heap from new. Calling .intern() returns the pooled one.

Why is String a popular HashMap key?

It's immutable (the key can't change after insertion), its hashCode is cached after the first call, and equals/hashCode are correctly implemented.

Why are passwords often kept in char[] rather than String?

A String can't be wiped and may linger in memory (and the pool) until GC, appearing in heap dumps. A char array can be overwritten with zeros right after use.

05OOP Java

Classes, objects, static and final

A class is a recipe card; an object is one dish made from it. Instance fields belong to each dish, static fields belong to the recipe card itself.

In Ramu's kitchen

The recipe card for Masala Chai says: water, milk, tea leaves, sugar level. Each cup made from it has its own sugar level (instance field). But "total cups sold today" is written once on the card itself, shared by all cups (static field). "Tea must be boiled at 100°C" is printed in ink and can never change (final).

The four access levels

ModifierSame classSame packageSubclass (other package)Everywhere
private✓✗✗✗
(default / package-private)✓✓✗✗
protected✓✓✓✗
public✓✓✓✓

The three meanings of final

final variable
Assign once

A final reference can't point elsewhere, but the object can still change: final List<String> l still allows l.add().

final method
Can't override

Subclasses must use it as is. Used for security-critical or template steps.

final class
Can't extend

String, Integer and records are final, so nobody can subclass and break their guarantees.

Initialisation order (a favourite tricky question)

  1. Class loads, onceStatic fields and static { } blocks run in source order (parent class first).
  2. Each newMemory is zeroed, then the parent constructor runs (via super()), then instance field initialisers and { } blocks, then the rest of the constructor body.
Lock it in

Static = the recipe card. Instance = the cup.

Static members are per class, instance members per object. Constructors chain with this(...)/super(...) as the first line. Statics first, parents first.

Interview questions

Can a static method access instance variables?

Not directly: there's no this in a static context. It can access them through an object reference passed in or created inside it.

Can we override a static method?

No. A static method with the same signature in a subclass hides the parent's; which one runs depends on the reference's declared type at compile time, not the object type. Overriding (runtime polymorphism) applies only to instance methods.

What's the difference between overloading and overriding?

Overloading: same method name, different parameter list, in the same class; resolved at compile time. Overriding: subclass provides a new body for an inherited instance method with the same signature; resolved at runtime by the object's actual type.

Next: Interfaces, abstract classes, records, enums, sealed →
06OOP Java

Interfaces, abstract classes, records, enums and sealed types

An interface says what something can do; an abstract class shares how it's done. Records, enums and sealed types are modern shortcuts for data, fixed sets and closed hierarchies.

In Ramu's kitchen

"Anyone who can Deliver" is a job description: Swiggy, Zomato, or Ramu's nephew on a cycle can all do it, however different they are (interface). "Beverage" is a half-written recipe: every beverage is poured into a cup the same way, but how it's brewed is left to Chai, Coffee, Lassi (abstract class). The menu's sizes are only Small, Medium and Large, nothing else (enum). An order slip is just data (record).

InterfaceAbstract class
RepresentsA capability: "can do"A partial base: "is a kind of"
Multiple?A class can implement manyCan extend only one
StateOnly static final constantsAny fields
ConstructorsNoYes (called by subclasses)
Methodsabstract, default, static, private (Java 9+)Any, abstract or concrete
Use whenUnrelated classes share a contract; you want to swap implementations (DI)Closely related classes share code and state

Modern Java data types

Interview tip

When asked "interface or abstract class?", say: prefer interfaces for the contract (it keeps classes free to extend something else and makes mocking and DI easy), and add an abstract base class only to share real code between closely related implementations. Mention that Spring injects by interface type.

Common trap

The diamond problem with default methods: if a class implements two interfaces with the same default method, it must override it and can pick one with A.super.method(). Java never silently guesses.

Lock it in

Interface = can-do. Abstract = is-a, half-built. Record = data. Enum = fixed list. Sealed = closed family.

Sealed types + records + pattern-matching switch = exhaustive, compiler-checked handling of every case.

Interview questions

Why were default methods added in Java 8?

To evolve interfaces without breaking existing implementations. Collection needed stream() and forEach(); adding abstract methods would have broken every collection class ever written, so they were added as defaults.

Can a record have extra methods or fields?

It can have extra methods, static fields and static methods, and a compact or custom constructor. It can't declare extra instance fields, can't extend another class (it implicitly extends java.lang.Record), and its fields are final. It can implement interfaces.

Why is an enum a good way to write a Singleton?

The JVM guarantees exactly one instance per constant, it's thread-safe by class initialisation, and it's safe against reflection and serialization attacks that can break other singleton styles.

Next: equals, hashCode and immutability →
07OOP Java

equals, hashCode, compareTo and immutability

If two objects are equal, they must have the same hashCode. Break that rule and HashMap and HashSet silently lose your data.

In Ramu's kitchen

Spice jars are stored on racks by the first letter of the label (the hash code), and inside a rack Ramu reads labels to find the exact jar (equals). If two jars both say "Haldi" but somebody files one under "H" and the other under "T", Ramu will look under "H", never find the second jar, and buy a duplicate. That's what happens when equal objects return different hash codes.

The contract

equals must be reflexive (a = a), symmetric (a = b ⇔ b = a), transitive, consistent, and x.equals(null) is false. hashCode: equal objects ⇒ equal hash codes. (Unequal objects may share a hash code; that's a collision, which is allowed.)

Common trap

Mutating a field used in hashCode while the object is inside a HashSet or used as a HashMap key. Its bucket no longer matches its hash, so contains and remove fail and the entry leaks. Keys should be immutable.

Comparable vs Comparator

How to make a class immutable

  1. Make the class finalso no subclass can add mutable state.
  2. All fields private finalassigned once in the constructor.
  3. No setters; "withX" methods return a new object instead.
  4. Defensive copiesof mutable inputs and outputs: this.items = List.copyOf(items).
  5. Or use a record, then still copy mutable components like lists in the compact constructor.
Lock it in

Same label, same rack.

Override equals and hashCode together, from the same fields. Map keys should be immutable. Comparable = one natural order; Comparator = any number of orders.

Interview questions

What is the difference between == and equals()?

== compares primitive values or, for objects, whether two references point to the same object. equals() compares logical equality as defined by the class; Object's default is the same as ==.

Can two unequal objects have the same hashCode?

Yes, that's a collision and it's legal; the map then uses equals within the bucket. Many collisions make lookups slower (O(log n) after treeification), so a good hash spreads values evenly.

Why are immutable objects good for concurrency?

Their state can't change after construction, so they can be shared between threads with no locks and no visibility problems (final fields are safely published by the Java memory model).

Next: Exceptions done right →
08OOP Java

Exceptions done right

Checked exceptions are problems the caller should plan for; unchecked exceptions are bugs or unrecoverable conditions. Errors are the JVM itself in trouble.

In Ramu's kitchen

"The milk supplier might not come" is a known risk; the recipe must say what to do (checked exception: the compiler forces you to handle or declare it). "The chef put salt instead of sugar" is a mistake; you fix the chef, not write a plan for it (unchecked). "The building is on fire" is not your recipe's problem (Error).

Do

Catch the most specific type. Keep the cause (new X(msg, e)). Use try-with-resources. Throw early (validate inputs), catch late (at a boundary that can act).

Don't

Catch Throwable/Exception and ignore it. Use exceptions for normal control flow. Return from finally (it hides the exception). Log and rethrow at every layer (duplicate logs).

Common trap

Spring's @Transactional rolls back only on unchecked exceptions by default. A checked exception will commit the transaction unless you add rollbackFor = Exception.class. See Spring Boot · Chapter 16.

Lock it in

Plan for checked, fix unchecked, flee from Error.

try-with-resources for anything closable. Wrap with cause, never swallow. finally always runs (except System.exit or a JVM crash).

Interview questions

What's the difference between throw and throws?

throw is a statement that throws an exception object right now. throws in a method signature declares which checked exceptions the method may pass up to its caller.

What happens if both try and finally return a value?

The finally value wins and any exception from try is discarded. That's why returning from finally is considered a bug.

What are suppressed exceptions?

In try-with-resources, if the body throws and then close() also throws, the close exception is attached to the main one as "suppressed" (e.getSuppressed()) instead of replacing it.

Next: Generics, wildcards and type erasure →
09OOP Java

Generics, wildcards and type erasure

Generics let the compiler check what goes into a container, so you get type errors at compile time instead of ClassCastException at runtime.

In Ramu's kitchen

A jar labelled "Spices only" (Jar<Spice>) stops anyone from putting sugar in it. A helper who only takes things out to taste can accept any jar of any kind of spice (? extends Spice). A helper who only puts chilli in can use a jar of chilli, of spices, or of anything at all (? super Chilli).

PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super

Type erasure

Generics exist only at compile time. The compiler checks types, inserts casts, and then erases T to its bound (usually Object). At runtime List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class. Consequences:

No new T()

T is unknown at runtime. Pass a Supplier<T> or Class<T> instead.

No instanceof List<String>

Only instanceof List<?> works.

No overloads that differ only by type argument

f(List<String>) and f(List<Integer>) erase to the same signature.

No primitives

List<int> isn't allowed; boxing is needed.

Lock it in

PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

Generics = compile-time safety, erased at runtime. Read from ? extends, write to ? super.

Interview questions

Is List<Integer> a subtype of List<Number>?

No. Generics are invariant. If it were, you could add a Double to a list of Integers through the Number reference. Use List<? extends Number> to accept both. (Arrays are covariant, which is why Object[] a = new String[1]; a[0] = 1; throws ArrayStoreException.)

What is type erasure and why did Java choose it?

The compiler removes generic type information after checking it, replacing type parameters with their bounds and adding casts. It was chosen for backward compatibility: generic code from Java 5 runs alongside and on the same JVM as pre-generics code.

The Collections map and Big-O cheat sheet

Ask three questions: do I need order, do I need uniqueness, do I look things up by key? The answers pick the collection.

In Ramu's kitchen

The ticket rail where orders are clipped in arrival order is a List (order, duplicates OK). The guest list of loyalty members is a Set (each person once). The spice rack where you find a jar by its label is a Map (key → value). The "next order to cook" queue, with VIPs jumping ahead, is a PriorityQueue.

Choosing in 10 seconds

default list
ArrayList

Contiguous array: cache-friendly and fast. LinkedList almost never wins in practice.

stack / queue

Faster than Stack (legacy, synchronized) and LinkedList. push/pop, offer/poll.

lookup by key

Lock it in

Rail, guest list, spice rack, VIP queue.

List = ordered with duplicates, Set = unique, Map = key → value, Queue = process in order. Default to ArrayList, HashMap, ArrayDeque.

Interview questions

ArrayList vs LinkedList: which is faster to insert in the middle?

On paper LinkedList is O(1) once you're at the node, but finding the position is O(n) and its nodes are scattered in memory. ArrayList shifts elements with a fast System.arraycopy, so in practice it's usually faster even for middle inserts unless the list is huge and you already hold an iterator.

Difference between HashMap and Hashtable?

Hashtable is legacy: every method synchronized (slow), no null keys or values. HashMap is unsynchronized and allows one null key. For thread safety use ConcurrentHashMap, not Hashtable.

Next: HashMap internals →
11Collections

HashMap internals: the most asked Java question

An array of buckets; the key's hash picks the bucket; equals finds the key inside it. Too many keys? Double the array. Too many in one bucket? Turn it into a tree.

In Ramu's kitchen

Ramu's spice rack has 16 numbered slots. To store a jar, he works out a number from its label and puts it in that slot. If two labels land in the same slot, he hangs the second jar under the first (a chain). When the rack is 75% full, he buys a rack twice as big and re-sorts everything. If one slot ever has a long dangle of 8 jars, he arranges that slot alphabetically so finding a jar takes fewer looks (a tree).

Step by step: put(key, value)

  1. HashCall key.hashCode() (null key → hash 0, bucket 0) and spread it: h ^ (h >>> 16) so the high bits influence the bucket too.
  2. Index(n - 1) & hash. Capacity is always a power of two, so this bit-mask is a fast modulo.
  3. Empty bucket?Place a new node there. Done.
  4. Occupied?Walk the chain. If a node has the same hash and equals the key, replace its value (and return the old one). Otherwise append a new node at the tail.
  5. TreeifyIf the chain reaches 8 nodes (and the table has ≥ 64 slots), convert that bucket to a red-black tree. If the table is smaller, resize instead. Trees shrink back to lists at 6.
  6. ResizeIf size exceeds capacity × loadFactor, double the table. Each node either stays at index i or moves to i + oldCapacity, depending on one bit of its hash, so no rehashing is needed.
LiveHashMap visualizer: put keys, watch buckets, collisions and resize

Why it matters: a bad hashCode destroys performance

Interview tip

If you know roughly how many entries you'll store, size the map upfront: HashMap.newHashMap(10_000) (Java 19+) creates a map that holds 10,000 entries without resizing. The older new HashMap<>(10_000) sets capacity, which resizes at 75% of the rounded-up size.

Common trap

Using HashMap from several threads. Concurrent puts can lose entries, and in Java 7 a concurrent resize could even create a cycle and hang get() forever. Use ConcurrentHashMap (22).

Lock it in

16 slots, 0.75 full, 8 becomes a tree, double when crowded.

hash → spread → &(n-1) → bucket → equals. Average O(1), worst O(log n) since Java 8.

Interview questions

Why is HashMap capacity always a power of two?

So the bucket index can be computed with a bitwise AND (hash & (n-1)), which is much faster than modulo, and so resize can split each bucket into "stay" and "move by oldCap" using a single bit. The constructor rounds any requested capacity up to the next power of two.

Why treeify at 8 and untreeify at 6?

With a decent hash function, the chance of 8 entries in one bucket is about 1 in 10 million (Poisson distribution), so trees appear only with bad hashes or attacks. The gap between 8 and 6 avoids flipping back and forth when the count hovers around the threshold.

What happens with a null key?

HashMap allows one null key, stored in bucket 0 with hash 0. ConcurrentHashMap and TreeMap (natural ordering) don't allow null keys.

How does get() work?

Compute the same spread hash, go to index hash & (n-1), check the first node (hash equal and key == or equals), then walk the list or search the tree. Return the value or null.

Next: Iterators, TreeMap, LinkedHashMap, PriorityQueue →
12Collections

Iterators, sorted maps, LRU and heaps

The specialised collections solve classic interview problems in one line: TreeMap for ranges, LinkedHashMap for LRU, PriorityQueue for top-K.

In Ramu's kitchen

A chef counting tickets on the rail while a waiter clips a new one on will lose count; the kitchen rule is "stop and shout" (fail-fast iterator). The price board sorted by price lets Ramu answer "cheapest dish above ₹50" instantly (TreeMap). The VIP bell always serves the most important order next (PriorityQueue).

Fail-fast iterators and ConcurrentModificationException

Concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList) have weakly consistent / fail-safe iterators: they never throw CME, but may not show changes made during iteration.

TreeMap: sorted keys and range queries

LinkedHashMap as an LRU cache

The from-scratch HashMap + doubly-linked-list version, with a live simulator, is in System Design · Chapter 4.

PriorityQueue: top-K in O(n log k)

Lock it in

Remove with removeIf. Ranges with TreeMap. LRU with LinkedHashMap. Top-K with a size-k heap.

Interview questions

What is the difference between fail-fast and fail-safe iterators?

Fail-fast (ArrayList, HashMap) track a modification count and throw ConcurrentModificationException if the collection changes outside the iterator. Fail-safe / weakly consistent (concurrent collections) iterate over a snapshot or tolerate changes and never throw.

HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap?

HashMap: no order, O(1). LinkedHashMap: keeps insertion (or access) order with a doubly linked list through the entries, O(1), slightly more memory. TreeMap: sorted by key with a red-black tree, O(log n), supports range queries.

Next: Part 4 · Functional Java →

Part 4 · Chapters 13 to 15

Functional Java: lambdas, streams and the modern language

Java 8 changed how Java is written, and every LTS since (11, 17, 21, 25) added more. Interviewers expect you to write a stream pipeline fluently and to know what changed in recent versions.

Lambdas and functional interfacesStreams: pipelines, laziness, collectorsModern Java: 8 to 25
13Functional

Lambdas and functional interfaces

A lambda is a short way to pass "a piece of behaviour" as a value. It fills in the one abstract method of a functional interface.

In Ramu's kitchen

Instead of hiring a whole new chef (a class) every time he needs "add extra ginger", Ramu writes the instruction on a sticky note and hands it to whichever chef is free. The sticky note is a lambda; the slot on the chef's clipboard that accepts exactly one instruction is the functional interface.

The six interfaces to know by heart

InterfaceMethodShapeExample
Supplier<T>get()() → T() -> new Order()
Consumer<T>accept(t)T → voido -> log.info(o)
Function<T,R>apply(t)T → ROrder::total
Predicate<T>test(t)T → booleano -> o.total() > 100
BiFunction<T,U,R>apply(t,u)(T,U) → R(a, b) -> a + b
UnaryOperator<T> / BinaryOperator<T>applyT → T / (T,T) → TString::trim, Integer::sum
Effectively final

A lambda can read local variables from the surrounding method only if they're never reassigned. The lambda captures the value, and allowing changes would create confusing races between threads. Fields and objects' contents can still change.

Lock it in

Supply, Consume, Function, Predicate.

A lambda implements the single abstract method of a functional interface. Captured locals must be effectively final.

Interview questions

Is a lambda the same as an anonymous class?

No. A lambda doesn't create a new scope (this refers to the enclosing object), can only implement functional interfaces, and is compiled with invokedynamic rather than generating a separate .class file per use, which is lighter.

Can a functional interface have default methods?

Yes, any number of default and static methods; it must have exactly one abstract method. Predicate.and, Function.andThen are default methods.

Next: Streams: pipelines, laziness, collectors →
14Functional

Streams: pipelines, laziness and collectors

A stream is an assembly line: a source, some intermediate steps, and one terminal step. Nothing happens until the terminal step pulls items through, one at a time.

In Ramu's kitchen

Ramu's assembly line has stations: wash → peel → chop → fry → plate. Potatoes don't all get washed first and then all peeled; each potato goes down the whole line before the next. And if the order is "just 3 plates of fries", the line stops after the third plate: the rest of the sack is never touched. That's laziness and short-circuiting.

LiveWatch laziness: items flow one by one, and limit() stops the line early

The collectors interviewers love

map vs flatMap

map: one in, one out

orders.map(Order::lines) gives a Stream<List<Line>>: a stream of lists.

flatMap: one in, many out, flattened

orders.flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream()) gives a Stream<Line>.

Optional: say "maybe empty" in the type

Parallel streams: careful

Common trap

.parallelStream() splits work over the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool() (cores - 1 threads). It helps only for large, CPU-heavy, independent work on easily splittable sources (arrays, ArrayList). It hurts for small lists, LinkedList, I/O calls (one slow call blocks the shared pool for the whole JVM), and any code with shared mutable state. In a web server, it's usually the wrong tool.

Lock it in

Source, steps, one terminal. Nothing runs until the terminal.

Streams are lazy, single-use and don't change the source. Use toMap with a merge function, groupingBy for buckets, primitive streams for numbers.

Interview questions

Intermediate vs terminal operations?

Intermediate (filter, map, flatMap, sorted, distinct, limit, peek) return a stream and are lazy. Terminal (collect, forEach, reduce, count, findFirst, anyMatch, toList) trigger processing and end the stream. Short-circuiting ones (limit, findFirst, anyMatch) can stop early, even on infinite streams.

findFirst vs findAny?

findFirst returns the first element in encounter order. findAny may return any element, which lets parallel streams return whichever finishes first. In sequential streams they usually behave the same.

Find the second highest salary with streams.

emps.stream().map(Employee::salary).distinct().sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).skip(1).findFirst() returns an Optional. Mention that a SQL query with OFFSET 1 or DENSE_RANK is better when the data is in a database.

What does peek() do and when should you use it?

It runs an action on each element as it passes, without changing it. It's meant for debugging; don't rely on it for side effects because with laziness or short-circuiting it may not run for every element.

Next: Modern Java: 8 to 25 →
15Functional

Modern Java: what changed from 8 to 25

Java ships every six months, with a long-term-support (LTS) release every two years: 8, 11, 17, 21, 25. Know the headline features of each LTS.

In Ramu's kitchen

Ramu's kitchen gets new equipment every season. Most of it is small (a better peeler), but every few years there's a big upgrade the whole chain adopts (an LTS). Interviewers ask "what version do you use and what do you like in it?": have one or two features ready per LTS.

What's new in Java 25 (LTS, September 2025)

JEP 519
Compact object headers

Object headers shrink from 12 to 8 bytes on 64-bit, cutting heap use for object-heavy apps. Opt in with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders.

JEP 514/515
AOT ergonomics and method profiling

Easier ahead-of-time caches that store class loading and JIT profiles from a training run, so services warm up faster.

JEP 521
Generational Shenandoah

The low-pause Shenandoah GC gets a young/old split, now a product feature.

still preview
Structured concurrency, primitive patterns, stable values

Good to name, not to depend on in production. See 22 for structured concurrency.

Interview tip

"Why upgrade from 8/11 to 21 or 25?" A strong answer names one productivity win (records, pattern matching), one performance win (virtual threads for blocking I/O, better GCs, compact headers) and one ecosystem reason (Spring Boot 3+ needs Java 17, Boot 4 is built for 17-25).

Lock it in

8 lambdas · 11 var + HttpClient · 17 records + sealed · 21 virtual threads + patterns · 25 scoped values + flexible constructors.

Interview questions

Is var dynamic typing?

No. The type is inferred at compile time and fixed; var x = 5; x = "a"; doesn't compile. It's only for local variables (and lambda parameters), not fields, method parameters or return types.

What's the difference between a preview feature and a final one?

Preview features are complete but may still change; you need --enable-preview to compile and run them, and they may change in the next release. Final features are permanent parts of the language.

16Concurrency

Processes, threads and the thread lifecycle

A process is a running program with its own memory; a thread is one path of execution inside it. Threads share the heap, which makes them fast to coordinate and easy to break.

In Ramu's kitchen

A process is the entire restaurant: building, stove, fridge, ingredients. When you run a Java program, the operating system opens one restaurant for it with its own private memory. A thread is one chef working inside. Every restaurant opens with at least one chef (the main thread). Multithreading is hiring more chefs so several dishes cook at the same time, all sharing the same kitchen. Two chefs grabbing the same pan is where the trouble starts.

Process (the restaurant)Thread (a chef)
What is it?A running program, e.g. your whole Java appOne path of execution inside a process
MemoryIts own private memory; processes don't shareShares the heap with other threads; has its own stack
Cost to createHeavy: opening a new restaurantLighter: hiring one more chef (~1 MB stack for a platform thread)
CommunicationHard: sockets, pipes, filesEasy: shared objects. Also where bugs come from.
One crashesOthers unaffectedAn uncaught exception kills that thread; an OOM can take down the process
Concurrency vs parallelism

Concurrency: several tasks in progress at once, maybe taking turns on one core (one chef juggling three pots). Parallelism: tasks literally running at the same instant on different cores (three chefs, three stoves). Threads give you concurrency; multiple cores turn it into parallelism.

The thread lifecycle

join()

"Pause my thread until that thread finishes." The head chef won't send the dish out until the sauce chef is done.

sleep(ms)

Pause the current thread. Keeps any locks it holds.

wait() / notify()

Called inside synchronized on the same object. wait() releases the lock and sleeps until notified. Low-level: prefer java.util.concurrent tools.

interrupt()

A polite "please stop" flag. Blocking calls throw InterruptedException; your code should finish up and exit.

Daemon threads

Background helpers (setDaemon(true)) that don't keep the JVM alive; e.g. GC threads.

Priority

setPriority(1..10) is only a hint to the OS. Never rely on it for correctness.

Lock it in

Hired, clocked in, waiting for the oven, gone home.

NEW → RUNNABLE → (BLOCKED / WAITING / TIMED_WAITING) → TERMINATED. sleep keeps locks, wait releases them.

Interview questions

Difference between sleep() and wait()?

sleep is a static Thread method, can be called anywhere, keeps held locks, and resumes after the time. wait is an Object method, must be called while holding that object's monitor (inside synchronized), releases the monitor, and resumes on notify/notifyAll, timeout or interrupt. Always call wait in a loop that re-checks the condition (spurious wakeups).

How do you stop a thread?

Cooperatively: call interrupt() (or set a volatile flag) and have the thread check Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() and handle InterruptedException by cleaning up and returning. Thread.stop() was deprecated and removed because it could leave objects half-updated.

Next: Creating threads: Thread vs Runnable →
17Concurrency

Creating threads: Thread, Runnable and Callable

The work always lives in a run() method; only start() creates a new thread. Prefer Runnable (or Callable) tasks handed to a pool.

In Ramu's kitchen

Extending Thread is like welding a recipe to one specific chef: that chef can only ever make that dish and can't take on any other identity. Implementing Runnable is writing the recipe on a card: any chef can pick it up, and later a whole team of reusable chefs (a thread pool) can share a stack of cards.

Classic trap: start() vs run()

Calling chef.run() creates no new thread: the main thread just runs the method like any normal call. Only start() asks the JVM to spin up a new thread. Calling the chef's phone (run()) isn't the same as the chef showing up to work (start()). And calling start() twice throws IllegalThreadStateException.

Why Runnable wins

Inheritance stays free

Your class can still extend something else.

Separation of concerns

The task (what to do) is separate from the worker (how it runs): easier to test.

Pools expect it

Executors accept Runnable and Callable tasks, not Thread subclasses.

Lambda-friendly

A task can be one clean line.

Runnable vs Callable

RunnableCallable<V>
Methodvoid run()V call() throws Exception
Returns a value?NoYes, via a Future
Checked exceptions?Must catch insideMay throw; surfaced by Future.get() as ExecutionException
Lock it in

Recipe on a card, not welded to a chef.

Write tasks as Runnable / Callable, run them on a pool, and remember start() ≠ run().

Interview questions

What happens if you call run() instead of start()?

The method runs synchronously on the calling thread; no new thread is created, so there is no concurrency. Printing Thread.currentThread().getName() inside would show "main".

What happens to an uncaught exception in a thread?

That thread terminates and the exception goes to its UncaughtExceptionHandler (by default, printed to stderr). Other threads keep running. In an ExecutorService with submit(), the exception is captured in the Future and only seen when you call get(), which is a common source of "silent" failures.

Next: Race conditions, synchronized, volatile, atomics →
18Concurrency

Race conditions, synchronized, volatile and atomics

When threads read and write shared data without coordination, updates get lost. Locks give one-at-a-time access; volatile gives visibility; atomics give lock-free single-variable updates.

In Ramu's kitchen

Two chefs read the order board: "3 pizzas left to make". Both grab ingredients, both make a pizza, and both walk back and write "2 pizzas left", because both did the maths from the old number they saw. Two pizzas were made but the board only dropped by one. That's a race condition.

The fix: the board now has a marker with a key attached. You may only update the board while holding the marker, and only one chef can hold it. Updates can no longer overlap.

LiveRace condition simulator: two threads, counter++ step by step

Synchronized method vs synchronized block

Rule of thumb

Lock the smallest section that touches shared data, and always use the same lock object for the same data. Locks only work if everyone agrees to use the same marker. Java monitors are reentrant: a thread holding a lock can enter another synchronized method on the same object without deadlocking itself.

The Java Memory Model in one picture: visibility

Atomics: lock-free counters

ToolAtomicityVisibilityBlocks?Use for
synchronized✓✓yescompound actions on several fields
volatile✗ (single read/write only)✓noflags, publish a reference once
AtomicX✓ one variable✓no (CAS)counters, sequence numbers
ReentrantLock✓✓yes, with tryLock/timeoutwhen you need fairness, timeouts, conditions
Lock it in

counter++ is read, add, write. Three steps, so two chefs can collide.

synchronized = one at a time + visibility. volatile = visibility only. Atomic = lock-free single variable. Best of all: don't share mutable state (immutable objects, confinement).

Interview questions

What is a race condition?

When the correctness of a result depends on the timing of threads accessing shared mutable data, e.g. two threads doing check-then-act (if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)) or read-modify-write (count++) without synchronization.

Does volatile make count++ thread-safe?

No. volatile guarantees each read sees the latest write, but count++ is still three separate operations, so two threads can read the same value and both write value+1. Use AtomicInteger or a lock.

What is CAS?

Compare-and-swap: a single CPU instruction that sets a memory location to a new value only if it still holds the expected old value, returning whether it succeeded. Atomic classes loop on CAS until it succeeds. It avoids blocking but can suffer the ABA problem (solved with AtomicStampedReference).

Why is double-checked locking broken without volatile?

The write of the singleton reference can be reordered before the constructor finishes, so another thread could see a non-null but half-built object. Declaring the field volatile forbids that reordering. (Simpler: use an enum or a holder class.)

Next: Deadlock, livelock and starvation →
19Concurrency

Deadlock, livelock and starvation

A deadlock is two or more threads each waiting for a lock the other holds, forever. No crash, no error, just a frozen program.

In Ramu's kitchen

A dish needs both the frying pan and the spatula. Chef A grabs the pan. At the same moment Chef B grabs the spatula. Chef A waits for the spatula ("I won't let go of my pan!"); Chef B waits for the pan ("I won't let go of my spatula!"). Both follow the rules, both wait forever. The kitchen is frozen.

LivePan and spatula: run both chefs, then fix it with lock ordering

The four ingredients (Coffman conditions)

1
Mutual exclusion

Only one holder per lock.

2
Hold and wait

Holding one lock while asking for another.

3
No preemption

Locks can't be forcibly taken away.

4
Circular wait

A waits for B, B waits for A. Break this one with a global lock order.

Livelock

Two chefs keep politely stepping aside for each other in a corridor: both active, neither progressing. Fix with random back-off.

Starvation

One chef never gets the stove because others always grab it first. Fix with fair locks (new ReentrantLock(true)) or bounded queues.

Lock it in

Pan before spatula, always.

Deadlock needs all four conditions; break circular wait with lock ordering, or use tryLock with timeouts. Diagnose with a thread dump.

Interview questions

How would you prevent deadlock in a bank transfer between two accounts?

Always lock the two accounts in a consistent global order, e.g. by account id: lock the smaller id first, then the larger, regardless of transfer direction. Alternatively use tryLock with timeout and retry, or avoid application locks entirely with a single database transaction using SELECT … FOR UPDATE in id order.

Can a deadlock happen with a single lock?

Not with Java's reentrant monitors on the same thread. But a thread can block forever waiting on itself in other ways, e.g. a task submitted to a single-thread executor that waits for another task submitted to the same executor (thread-starvation deadlock).

Next: Executors and thread pools →
20Concurrency

Executors and thread pools

Don't create a thread per task; hire a fixed team and put tasks on a queue. ThreadPoolExecutor's core → queue → max → reject order is a top SDE-2 question.

In Ramu's kitchen

The old way: every time an order arrives, hire a brand-new chef, they cook one dish, then fire them. Absurdly wasteful. A thread pool is the sane way: hire a fixed team of, say, 4 chefs once. Orders go onto a ticket rail (a queue). Whenever a chef is free, they grab the next ticket. On a busy night with 100 orders, still just 4 calm chefs working through the rail.

How ThreadPoolExecutor decides what to do with a new task

LiveThreadPoolExecutor: core 2, queue 3, max 4. Submit tasks and watch

How many threads?

CPU-bound
≈ number of cores

Image resizing, encryption, parsing. More threads just add context switching. Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors().

I/O-bound
cores × (1 + wait / compute)

A task that waits 90 ms on a DB and computes 10 ms: 8 cores × 10 = ~80 threads. Or use virtual threads.

bounded by downstream
≤ connection pool

100 threads sharing a 10-connection DB pool means 90 threads waiting. Size them together.

Lock it in

Core, then queue, then max, then reject.

Always bounded queue, named threads, explicit rejection policy, and call shutdown(). Size CPU pools to cores and I/O pools to waiting time.

Interview questions

Explain the ThreadPoolExecutor parameters.

corePoolSize (threads kept alive), maximumPoolSize (upper limit), keepAliveTime (idle time before extra threads die), workQueue (where tasks wait), threadFactory (creates/names threads), and RejectedExecutionHandler (what to do when queue and max are full). New tasks go: start a core thread → else queue → else start a non-core thread up to max → else reject.

submit() vs execute()?

execute(Runnable) returns nothing; an exception goes to the thread's uncaught exception handler. submit() accepts Runnable or Callable and returns a Future; exceptions are stored inside it and rethrown (wrapped in ExecutionException) only when you call get().

shutdown() vs shutdownNow()?

shutdown stops accepting new tasks but finishes queued ones. shutdownNow also interrupts running tasks and returns the list of tasks that never started. Follow either with awaitTermination.

Next: CompletableFuture: async pipelines →
21Concurrency

CompletableFuture: async pipelines without blocking

A Future you can chain: "when this finishes, do that", combine several results, and handle errors, all without a thread sitting and waiting.

In Ramu's kitchen

With a plain Future, the head chef hands out a ticket and then stands at the counter staring until it's ready (get() blocks). With CompletableFuture he leaves a note on the ticket: "when the rice is done, add the dal; when both rice and curry are done, plate the thali; if anything burns, serve plain roti". Then he goes off to do other work.

MethodLikeUse when
thenApply(f)maptransform the result synchronously
thenCompose(f)flatMapthe next step is itself async (returns a CompletableFuture)
thenCombine(other, f)zipcombine two independent results
thenAccept / thenRunforEachside effect at the end
allOf(...) / anyOf(...)wait for all / firstfan-out over many calls
exceptionally / handle / whenCompletecatch / finallyrecover, or inspect result + error
orTimeout / completeOnTimeouttimeoutnever wait forever
Common trap

Without an executor argument, supplyAsync runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), shared by the whole JVM including parallel streams. Blocking I/O there starves everything else. Always pass your own I/O pool (or a virtual-thread executor). Also: join() throws unchecked CompletionException; get() throws checked ExecutionException.

Lock it in

Apply transforms, Compose chains, Combine joins, allOf waits.

Start independent work at the same time, pass your own executor, add a timeout and a fallback.

Interview questions

Future vs CompletableFuture?

Future only lets you check or block (get()). CompletableFuture can be completed manually, chained with callbacks, combined with others, and has built-in error handling and timeouts, enabling non-blocking pipelines.

thenApply vs thenApplyAsync?

thenApply runs the function on whichever thread completed the previous stage (or the caller, if already complete). thenApplyAsync submits it to an executor (the common pool, or the one you pass), which is useful when the next step is heavy.

Next: Locks, concurrent collections, virtual threads →
22Concurrency

java.util.concurrent toolbox and virtual threads

Use the ready-made tools: ConcurrentHashMap, BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch, Semaphore, ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock, and since Java 21, virtual threads for millions of blocking tasks.

In Ramu's kitchen

Ramu's kitchen has gadgets for every coordination problem: a ticket rail that makes chefs wait when empty (BlockingQueue), a countdown board "start serving when all 3 starters are ready" (CountDownLatch), 3 tokens for 3 stoves (Semaphore), and a menu board anyone can read but only one person can rewrite (ReadWriteLock).

ConcurrentHashMap

ToolKitchen pictureTypical use
BlockingQueue (Array/Linked)ticket rail: put waits if full, take waits if emptyproducer–consumer, back-pressure
CopyOnWriteArrayListreprint the whole list on every changemany reads, rare writes (listeners)
CountDownLatch(n)"serve when all n starters are ready"; single usewait for n tasks to finish / start together
CyclicBarrier(n)everyone waits at the pass until all n arrive; reusablephases of parallel work
Semaphore(n)n stove tokenslimit concurrent calls to a slow API
ReentrantLocka key you can try for, with timeouttryLock, fairness, multiple Conditions
ReentrantReadWriteLock / StampedLockmany readers or one writerread-heavy caches

ThreadLocal

A ThreadLocal gives each thread its own copy of a variable (each chef's own apron pocket). Spring uses it for the current transaction, security context and request attributes.

Common trap

In a thread pool the thread is reused, so a value left in a ThreadLocal leaks into the next request on that thread (wrong user!) and can leak memory. Always remove() in a finally. In Java 25 prefer ScopedValue, which is immutable and automatically ends with its scope.

Virtual threads (Java 21)

Great for

I/O-bound request handling: REST calls, DB queries, message consumers. Write simple blocking code, get reactive-like scalability.

Don't

Pool them (they're cheap; create one per task). Use them for CPU-heavy work (no speed-up). Forget the DB pool is still the limit: use a Semaphore or pool size.

Pinning

In Java 21–23 a virtual thread blocking inside synchronized pinned its carrier. Java 24 (JEP 491) fixed this for synchronized; native calls can still pin.

Structured concurrency (preview)

StructuredTaskScope treats subtasks as one unit: if one fails, the others are cancelled. Still a preview in Java 25.

Lock it in

Rail, countdown, tokens, read-many-write-one.

Use merge/compute on ConcurrentHashMap, bounded BlockingQueues for producer–consumer, and virtual threads for blocking I/O, not for CPU work.

Interview questions

How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety?

Java 7 used 16 segments each with its own lock. Java 8+ uses a Node array like HashMap: inserting into an empty bin uses CAS; otherwise it synchronizes on the bin's head node, so only one bucket is locked. Reads are lock-free using volatile reads. Size is tracked with LongAdder-style counter cells.

synchronized vs ReentrantLock?

Both are reentrant mutual-exclusion locks with the same memory semantics. ReentrantLock adds tryLock (with timeout), lockInterruptibly, optional fairness, and multiple Condition objects, but you must unlock in finally. synchronized is simpler and released automatically.

CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier?

CountDownLatch: one or more threads wait until a count reaches zero; other threads count down; it can't be reset. CyclicBarrier: a fixed number of threads wait for each other at a barrier point, then all proceed; it resets for reuse and can run a barrier action.

When would virtual threads not help?

CPU-bound work (cores are the limit), code limited by a small downstream resource (connection pools), and code relying heavily on ThreadLocal caches of expensive objects (one per virtual thread means millions).

Next: Spring Boot: insert 10,000 records in parallel →
23Concurrency in practice

Spring Boot in practice: insert 10,000 records with multithreading

Split the list into chunks, save each chunk on a pool thread in its own transaction, and wait for all of them. A very popular SDE-2 interview question.

In Ramu's kitchen

10,000 plates need to go from the kitchen to the storeroom. One waiter carrying one plate at a time takes all night. The smart way: stack the plates into trays of 500 (chunks) and let a team of 5 waiters (a thread pool) carry trays at the same time. Same plates, a fraction of the time. But the storeroom has only so many doors (database connections), so hiring 50 waiters wouldn't help.

The plan maps onto Spring's tools: chunking (split the list), ThreadPoolTaskExecutor (Spring's wrapper around the Executor framework), @Async ("run this method on a pool thread"), and CompletableFuture (the receipt that tells us when every chunk is done).

The #1 @Async trap

@Async (like @Transactional) works through a Spring proxy. If a method calls an @Async method in the same class (self-invocation), the proxy is bypassed and it silently runs on the same thread: no parallelism. That's exactly why the worker is a separate bean from the orchestrator below. Also: @Async methods must be public and return void, Future or CompletableFuture.

ApproachRough time for 10k rows*Notes
save() in a loop, one thread~20–40 sone transaction + round trip per row
saveAll() + batch_size, one thread~2–4 sbatching is the biggest win
Chunks on 5 threads + batching~0.6–1.2 sthis chapter
JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate / COPY~0.3–0.8 sno entity overhead; best for pure bulk loads

* Illustrative orders of magnitude on a local database; measure on yours.

Interview tip: say the trade-offs

Each chunk commits separately, so a failure in chunk 7 leaves chunks 1–6 saved: the job is not atomic. Mention how you'd handle it: idempotent upserts, a job-status table, retrying failed chunks, or Spring Batch (chunk-oriented processing with restart). For very large loads (millions of rows) or recurring jobs, Spring Batch or the database's bulk loader is the better answer. And the thread count is capped by the connection pool, not the CPU.

Lock it in

Trays of 500, five waiters, one door each.

Chunk → @Async worker in a separate bean → own @Transactional → allOf().join(). Turn on hibernate.jdbc.batch_size, use SEQUENCE ids, size Hikari ≥ threads.

Interview questions

Why not just use one @Transactional around all 10,000 inserts on many threads?

A Spring transaction is bound to one thread (via ThreadLocal) and one connection. Work on other threads doesn't join it. So either it's one thread with one big transaction (atomic, slower, huge persistence context: flush/clear every N rows), or several threads with one transaction each (faster, not atomic).

Why does GenerationType.IDENTITY break batching?

With IDENTITY the database generates the id on insert, and Hibernate needs that id immediately to manage the entity, so it must execute each INSERT right away instead of batching them. SEQUENCE lets Hibernate get ids ahead of time (allocationSize) and batch the inserts.

What happens if an exception is thrown in an @Async method?

With a CompletableFuture return type, the future completes exceptionally and join() rethrows it as CompletionException; that chunk's transaction rolls back. With void return, it goes to the AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler (default: logged), easy to miss.

Part 6 · Chapters 24 to 25

Under the hood: garbage collection and production troubleshooting

SDE-2 interviews often end with "your service is slow / out of memory in production, what do you do?". These two chapters give you the mental model and the commands.

Garbage collectionTroubleshooting a production JVM
24Under the hood

Garbage collection: who cleans the heap

The GC finds objects no live reference can reach and frees their memory. Most objects die young, so the heap is split into a young area cleaned often and an old area cleaned rarely.

In Ramu's kitchen

The cleaner doesn't ask "is this plate dirty?". He starts from what chefs are currently holding or pointing at and marks everything reachable from there. Anything unmarked is cleared. He cleans the prep counter (young generation) every few minutes because most things there are scraps used once. Plates that survive several cleanings get moved to the long-term shelf (old generation), which he cleans only occasionally because it's slow.

Generations

LiveGenerational GC: allocate objects, run minor GCs, watch promotion

Which collector?

CollectorFlagPause goalBest for
Serial-XX:+UseSerialGCstop-the-world, single threadtiny heaps, small containers, CLIs
Parallel-XX:+UseParallelGCthroughput over pausesbatch jobs
G1 (default since 9)-XX:+UseG1GCpredictable, ~200 ms target (MaxGCPauseMillis)most services
ZGC (generational in 21+)-XX:+UseZGCsub-millisecond, mostly concurrentlarge heaps, latency-critical APIs
Shenandoah (generational in 25)-XX:+UseShenandoahGClow pause, concurrent compactionlatency-sensitive (OpenJDK builds)

G1 splits the heap into equal regions (1–32 MB) and collects the regions with the most garbage first, hence "Garbage First".

Memory leaks in a garbage-collected language

Lock it in

Mark from the roots, sweep the rest. Clean the counter often, the shelf rarely.

Reachability, not ref-counting. Most objects die young. G1 is the default; ZGC for tiny pauses. Leaks = references you forgot to drop.

Interview questions

Can you force garbage collection?

System.gc() is only a request; the JVM may ignore it (and -XX:+DisableExplicitGC disables it). Calling it in application code is almost always a mistake.

What is a stop-the-world pause?

A phase where all application threads are paused so the GC can work safely (at safepoints). Modern collectors (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah) do most of their marking and compaction concurrently to keep these pauses short.

Strong, soft, weak and phantom references?

Strong: normal; never collected while reachable. Soft: collected only when memory is low (memory-sensitive caches). Weak: collected at the next GC once only weakly reachable (WeakHashMap keys, canonical maps). Phantom: used with a ReferenceQueue for post-mortem cleanup (Cleaner).

What is finalize() and why avoid it?

A method the GC might call before reclaiming an object. It's unpredictable, slow, can resurrect objects, and is deprecated for removal. Use try-with-resources or java.lang.ref.Cleaner.

25Under the hood

Troubleshooting a production JVM

High CPU? Take thread dumps. Memory climbing? Take a heap dump. Slow and spiky? Read the GC log. Then fix the code, not the flags.

In Ramu's kitchen

When the kitchen slows down, Ramu doesn't guess. He takes a photo of what every chef is doing right now (thread dump), a stock-take of the storeroom (heap dump), and checks the cleaner's logbook (GC log). Three photos a few seconds apart show who is stuck at the same stove.

SymptomLikely causeFirst tool
OutOfMemoryError: Java heap spaceleak or heap too small for the loadheap dump → Eclipse MAT "dominator tree"
OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceededheap almost full; GC runs nonstop, frees littleGC log, heap dump
OutOfMemoryError: Metaspaceclass-loader leak (redeploys), heavy proxiesjcmd VM.metaspace
OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native threadtoo many threads (unbounded pool)thread dump, count threads
100% CPUhot loop, regex backtracking, GC thrashingtop -H + thread dump
requests hang, CPU lowdeadlock, exhausted DB/HTTP pool, slow downstreamthread dumps (BLOCKED / WAITING on pool)
pod killed with exit 137 (OOMKilled)total memory (heap + metaspace + threads + direct buffers) > container limitNMT: -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary
LivePractice terminal: diagnose a slow Java service

The incident playbook (say this in interviews)

  1. StabiliseScale out or roll back first. Protect users before debugging.
  2. Look at metricsCPU, heap after GC, GC pause time, thread count, pool usage, p99 latency, error rate (Actuator + Micrometer + Grafana).
  3. Capture evidence3 thread dumps 5–10 s apart; a heap dump if memory is the issue; a 60 s JFR recording.
  4. Find the culpritSame stack in every dump = stuck or hot code. Dominator tree = what holds memory.
  5. Fix and preventFix the code; add a timeout, bound, or test; add an alert so you see it earlier next time.
Lock it in

Photo of chefs, stock-take, cleaner's logbook.

CPU → top -H + jstack. Memory → jstat + heap dump + MAT. Everything → jcmd and JFR.

Interview questions

Your Spring Boot service's memory keeps growing until it's OOM-killed. How do you investigate?

Check whether it's heap or native: if heap-after-GC keeps rising, it's a heap leak; take two heap dumps some time apart and compare the dominator trees in MAT (common: unbounded caches, static maps, ThreadLocals, huge sessions). If heap is flat but RSS grows, use Native Memory Tracking (threads, direct buffers, metaspace). Make sure MaxRAMPercentage leaves room for non-heap memory in the container.

What's in a thread dump?

For every thread: name, state (RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING…), the native id, the full stack trace, and the locks it holds or is waiting for. The JVM also reports detected deadlocks at the end.

R1Revision

The cheat sheet

Every concept in one or two lines, with the kitchen picture that helps you remember it.

The platform

ch 1 · JVM
How Java runs

javac → bytecode → class loader → interpreter + JIT. JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM. Universal recipe language.

ch 2 · memory
Stack vs heap

Notepad per chef, shelves for all. Stack: frames, locals, per thread. Heap: objects, shared. Always pass-by-value.

ch 3 · types
Wrappers

Integer cache −128..127: compare with equals. Never unbox a possible null. BigDecimal for money.

ch 4 · String
Strings

Laminated card. Immutable, literals pooled, hash cached. StringBuilder in loops.

Object-oriented Java

ch 5 · static
static and final

Recipe card vs cup. Static per class, instance per object. Final = no reassign / override / extend.

ch 5 · init
Init order

Parent static → child static → parent instance + constructor → child instance + constructor.

ch 6 · types
Interface vs abstract

Can-do contract vs half-built is-a. Records = data, enum = fixed set, sealed = closed family.

ch 7 · equals
equals and hashCode

Same label, same rack. Override together, same fields. Keys immutable. Comparator for extra orders.

ch 8 · errors
Exceptions

Plan for checked, fix unchecked, flee Error. try-with-resources. Wrap with cause.

ch 9 · generics
Generics

Compile-time safety, erased at runtime. PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Invariant.

Collections

ch 10 · choose
Which collection

Rail = List, guest list = Set, spice rack = Map, VIP bell = PriorityQueue. Default ArrayList, HashMap, ArrayDeque.

ch 11 · HashMap
HashMap internals

16 slots, 0.75 load, treeify at 8 (table ≥ 64), double on resize. hash ^ (h>>>16), index = h & (n−1).

ch 12 · iterate
Iterators and friends

Fail-fast CME → removeIf. TreeMap for ranges. LinkedHashMap(access order) = LRU. Size-k heap for top-K.

Functional Java

ch 13 · lambda
Lambdas

Sticky-note instruction. Implements the single abstract method. Supplier, Consumer, Function, Predicate.

ch 14 · streams
Streams

Assembly line. Lazy, single-use, never mutates source. groupingBy, toMap with merge, flatMap flattens.

ch 15 · versions
Modern Java

8 lambdas · 11 var/HttpClient · 17 records/sealed · 21 virtual threads/patterns · 25 scoped values.

Concurrency

ch 16 · threads
Thread lifecycle

NEW → RUNNABLE → BLOCKED / WAITING / TIMED_WAITING → TERMINATED. sleep keeps locks, wait releases.

ch 17 · create
Creating threads

Recipe on a card: Runnable/Callable on a pool. start() creates a thread, run() doesn't.

ch 18 · sync
Synchronization

counter++ = read, add, write. synchronized = atomic + visible; volatile = visible; Atomic = CAS.

ch 19 · deadlock
Deadlock

Pan before spatula. Four Coffman conditions; break circular wait with lock order or tryLock.

ch 20 · pools
Thread pools

Core → queue → max → reject. Bounded queue, named threads, CallerRunsPolicy. Size to cores or I/O wait.

ch 21 · async
CompletableFuture

Apply transforms, Compose chains, Combine joins, allOf waits. Own executor, timeout, fallback.

ch 22 · JUC
Concurrency toolbox

CHM merge/compute, BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch, Semaphore, ReadWriteLock. Virtual threads for I/O.

ch 23 · Spring
10,000-row insert

Trays of 500, five waiters. @Async worker bean, own @Transactional, allOf.join, batch_size, Hikari ≥ threads.

Under the hood

ch 24 · GC
Garbage collection

Mark from roots, sweep the rest. Young often, old rarely. G1 default, ZGC sub-ms pauses.

ch 25 · prod
Troubleshooting

CPU → top -H + jstack. Memory → jstat + heap dump + MAT. jcmd + JFR for everything.
